title: High cardinality — spoken follow-up
situation: In a technical discussion, a proposal uses customer identifiers as metric labels. You must answer aloud accurately without overstating the evidence.
instructions: Say aloud why customer identifiers must not become metric labels, and give the order of magnitude that makes it fail.

vocabulary.meaning: keeping the number of distinct label combinations bounded, because each combination becomes a separate stored series
the growth of stored time series when an unbounded value is used as a label, which degrades the whole metric store rather than one metric

expectedElements: The mechanism of series creation is explained
An order of magnitude is given, not just a warning
An alternative placement for the identifier is proposed
modelAnswer: Customer identifiers cannot be metric labels, and the mechanism matters more than the rule. Every distinct combination of labels creates a separate stored series. With a bounded label like status you get a handful. With a customer identifier you get one series per customer, so a hundred thousand customers means a hundred thousand series for a single metric. That does not degrade one dashboard; it degrades the whole metric store for everyone. The identifier belongs in a log line or a trace, where per-request evidence is expected and priced accordingly. How many distinct customers are we talking about?
commonMistakes: Stating the rule without explaining that each label combination becomes a series
Warning about cost without giving an order of magnitude
variants: Answer again when the proposal is to use a hashed identifier instead.
